explain.say: Most of the world's electricity, from coal, gas, nuclear and solar-thermal plants, comes from one loop of water and steam called the Rankine cycle, after the Scottish engineer William Rankine. The same water goes round and round, through four machines. Look at the loop.

explain.say: Now the real thing in 3D: a steam power plant. Follow the loop: the boiler makes steam, the turbine spins the generator, the condenser turns it back to water, and the feed pump sends it round again. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.

explain.say: Start at the pump. It pushes cold liquid water from the condenser pressure, 10 kilopascals, up to boiler pressure, 10 megapascals. Pumping a liquid takes very little work: v times delta P, about 10 kilojoules per kilogram. See the pump? Why is a liquid so much easier to pump than steam?

explain.say: Because its volume is tiny! Next, the boiler heats the water, boils it and superheats it to 500 degrees Celsius. That takes about 3172 kilojoules per kilogram, mostly from burning fuel or splitting atoms. See the boiler? Where does all that energy go next?

explain.say: Into the turbine! The steam expands through it, spinning the blades and a generator, giving about 1285 kilojoules per kilogram. It leaves as a wet mix, about 79 percent steam. Then the condenser cools it back to water, using river water or cooling towers. See the condenser closing the loop? Why not skip the condenser?

explain.say: Because pumping steam back up would cost far more work than pumping water. The efficiency is the net work over the heat in: 1285 minus 10, divided by 3172, about 40 percent. Wonderful! Real link: modern plants add reheat and very high pressures to reach about 45 percent. Exam tip: get every enthalpy from the steam tables carefully.

faq.q: How do I calculate Rankine cycle efficiency?
faq.a: Efficiency equals net work divided by heat added: turbine work minus pump work, divided by the boiler heat. Each is found from enthalpy differences in the steam tables.

faq.q: Why is the pump work in a Rankine cycle so small?
faq.a: Pump work is about specific volume times the pressure rise. Liquid water has a volume about a thousand times smaller than steam, so the work is tiny compared with the turbine work.
It adds heat at constant pressure, turning high-pressure water into hot superheated steam. This is where the fuel's energy enters the cycle.
High-pressure steam expands through rows of blades, spinning the shaft that drives the generator. This is where the cycle produces its work.

faq.q: Why does a power plant need a condenser?
faq.a: It turns the low-pressure steam back into water so the pump can return it cheaply. The low condenser pressure also lets the turbine extract more work. It is where the waste heat leaves.

facts: The Rankine cycle is named after the Scottish engineer William John Macquorn Rankine.
In a simple Rankine cycle, the pump work is typically around one percent of the turbine work.
